utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Interpreters are ready so we can resume our work. Mr. Dubuisson will you call the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14-1/T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. The appearances, please, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. And for the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Mikulicic, and along with my colleague Mr. Joka, we represent Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor, is there another witness you wish to call to the stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the Defence is calling the witness Viktor Maric. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric. Please read the solemn declaration that the usher is holding out for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may sit down. To begin with, you will answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic who is on your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I hope that you're comfortable, my name is Mikulicic and I represent the accused, Mr. Aleksovski, in this matter. I'm going to ask several questions and I would like to ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. For the beginning, Mr. Maric, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Podjele in the municipality of Busovaca on the 20th of March, 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: My ethnic background is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you religious?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you said that you were born in a village near Busovaca; where did you finish your elementary school?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: In Kaonik and four years, and in Katici another four. This was in the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you continue your schooling later?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes. I continued the secondary school for machinery in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, did you serve in the former JNA? Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: This was in 1975 in Vipava and Nova Gorica in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After, upon leaving the JNA, did you receive any rank?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you a regular soldier?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I was a border patrol soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, where did you get your first employment?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: This was in 1978, at the steelworks in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Until when did you work in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do, what was were you employed as?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I was a machine technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the steel mills in Zenica until 1992; in that period the war conflict had already started in the Republic of Croatia and earlier in Slovenia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, what did you do in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: In 1992 I joined the units, the defence units of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify this to us in more detail? When did you join and what type of unit was this?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The fact is that I think that as early as 1991 the village of Ravno was attacked by the JNA, and the Croats had already organised to help defend the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And later, after the attack on the village of Ravno, where were you? What type of military formation were you?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I was in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992, when defending the attacks by the JNA and the Serbian army, did only Croats take part or did also the Bosnian citizens of Muslim descent took up arms?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It was mostly the Croats, and there were very few Muslim volunteers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you somehow try to explain this to yourself?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: By following the media, the television, their official said this was not their war, that they had not yet been threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that if their leaders said this was not their war, they meant the war against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To your recollection, did the citizens of the Muslim ethnic background, and when did the citizens of Muslim ethnic background join this resistance of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but when it was obvious that the JNA is already attacking the territory where the Muslims were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, all this is going on in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the state authorities in Sarajevo did proclaim the state of war?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when this was, but I believe it was in April that they declared it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this for the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you tell us where did you stay after that, that is what units did you join?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I was in the HVO. I was involved in securing the main highways, the main communication lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you recall in which areas you were involved in these activities?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: This was in the area of the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the town of Busovaca or the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you mentioned that you were born in the village of Podjele, a village close to Busovaca, how far is it from the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It is about four-and-a-half kilometres away from the centre of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I assume that you are familiar with the situation as it was early in 1992 in the territory of the municipality -- '93 in the territory of the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, do you recall the events of late 1992 and early 1993 in the municipality of Busovaca? Were there some tensions which developed between the Croat and Muslim population in this area?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, you could feel that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe to us your recollections of these events?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The Muslim officials in the municipality of Busovaca distanced themselves, they became more separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at that time that the Muslim population started leaving this territory, the town of Busovaca and the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, this was frequent occurrence. There was a market in Busovaca over the weekend, and you could see that a number of people had left Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What part of the population was leaving the town in the municipality of Busovaca in this way?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: For the most part these were the citizens of the Muslim ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But a number of the people of Muslim ethnic background stayed in town?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall with regard to sex which people of which sex stayed and people of which sex left Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They mostly left from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What I mean is, were they mostly males who were leaving?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, it was mostly males.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, did you also notice that women and children were leaving town?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you interpret these departures? Why did you think these people were leaving?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: At that time we thought that they were getting organised in Kacuni, the neighbouring area, that they were attempting to organise themselves, something, so you could sense something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. In January of 1993 we know that Busovaca was attacked. Do you remember those events, and can you tell us when this took place?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, this was on 24 January 1993 and what preceded it was a killing of Ivica Petrovic and another policeman in Kacuni. And the following day a general attack on Busovaca ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From which directions was Busovaca attacked?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it came from the direction of Kacuni, Merdani, for the most part, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you mentioned those two locations, Kacuni and Merdani; what was the majority population of those two villages?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I know that in Merdani the population was 100 per cent Muslim; and Kacuni, I believe that it was about 80 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time you were a volunteer in the HVO. What was your duty, what was your task at the time, during the attack on Busovaca? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I was the driver of the HVO president, and in this role I performed these duties. This was, this also included taking care, to protect the population in the zone of responsibility of the HVO, and anything else that one could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you worked, that you were engaged in the protection of the population; can you tell me, Mr. Maric, immediately prior to these events, did also Croat displaced persons arrive from the neighbouring villages?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, given that these villages were close to the combat zones, it was probably about three or four hundred metres away, we needed to take care of the families who were arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall from which villages did Croat refugees arrive?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, this was Putis, Podjele, Gavrine Kuce, Loncari and the villages around Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are all these villages in the territory of the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, did you have an opportunity to talk to the people who were driven out of their homes? Did they tell you what happened?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were surprised, they could not comprehend at first what had happened to them. They were simply in a state of panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you who drove them away from their homes?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, since these were all neighbours before the war, they knew where the shooting was coming from, where the shells were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was that was shooting?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It was the Muslim units who were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The people who came from the surrounding villages to the town of Busovaca, where would they be put up?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: At first they were put up in this collective housing units in school buildings and later on a lot of people just took people into their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you were involved in these activities?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But primarily your job was to be the personal driver of the HVO president?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, do you know whether the HVO president at that time was a civilian or military person?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: He was a civilian person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his roles were, what his duties were?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I assume that it was the organisation of civilian life in these war time conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1993, was this the only work that you did, or did you move, were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: On 15th March 1993 I was appointed the person in charge of the civilian defence in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mean the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you told us that in your professional career you worked in the steel mill in Zenica, then you joined the HVO units as a volunteer and now you're telling us that you were appointed the commander of the civilian protection in the Busovaca municipality. Did you know, did you have any experience about how the civilian protection was supposed to function?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, I did not have any specific experience in that way, but you familiarise yourself very quickly in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the role of the civilian protection was?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The civilian protection has as its main function to organise civilian protection in terms of taking care of the refugees, to establish the units which would engage in activities that were important in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, one of the functions was also to establish the so-called work units, detachments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, when you came to the post of the civilian protection, did these activities include getting people who were to create lists of people who would be involved in particular duties there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, there were some lists available there, but people who were involved in the civilian protection at that time also took lists of people who were of the military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when you assumed the post at the civilian protection that you determined that the people on the list who were of Muslim ethnic background had left the territory of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, they were not there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you also have the lists of conscripts and recruits?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, those containing the lists of Muslim conscripts were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, does it mean that being involved in the activities of civilian protection you actually had no insight into who of the Muslim civilian protection recruits was there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: We then tried to compile a new list of the military conscripts who were at that time available in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you just tried to compile new lists?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many able-bodied male persons were there in Busovaca, how many military conscripts were there in the territory of the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I could not tell you the exact number, but very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Maric, when you performed your duties, what was the technique you used? How did you do this? For example, if you needed a certain number of people for a certain work, how did you do this technically, what did you do? Could you describe that please?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, at the request of the commander of the unit, of the HVO, a certain number of people were requested for specific duties along the lines, and then we would send out invitations using a courier, or a runner. Or if that was not possible, we would do this via the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you mentioned if that was not possible that you would use the military police. What situations did you resort to this second method of gathering people?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, we used this second method when there was combat and when this was, it was not, we were not able to use a courier or when the situation was extremely urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many men a work unit would be composed of?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, it depended, depending on the work to be done, the tasks set before the unit on the terrain, but they ranged from 10 to 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In what way did you organise the transport of these individuals who were to go on to do work on terrain? Did they go on foot, were they transported some way?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, we would collect them, there would be a checkpoint, and then transport would be organised by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who secured these, escorted these people?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The military police did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose, and please put me right if I'm wrong, that there were cases when individuals did not respond to the call up?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What would you do then, if somebody failed to turn up?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: We would apply certain measures, we would resort to everything that we could on the basis of the law, disciplinary measures, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there, could you resort to any other disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, detention measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you mentioned that the military police would escort these work units and that they were working on the terrain. Do you remember the locations they were sent to? Where did they work, in which areas?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, depending on the needs, they were usually the approach roads and bridges and defence lines, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned defence lines. Can you tell us, quote a few locations and villages in the vicinity of which you would have work units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They were Loncari, Podjele, Kula. There were some other localities, I can't think of them at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Loncari you said, Podjele and Kula. Would it be true to say that those villages, those positions were along the frontlines of the combat activities?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that along those locations there were objective threats, that their lives were threatened when they were doing their work?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How then did the military police guard these people, do you know?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well they would escort them to the place of work. They would assess the circumstances and the conditions; were the conditions were conducive to work at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were these duties performed during the day or the night?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, mostly at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when you performed your duties that there were any incidents which broke out while this work was going along the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, there were some sporadic incidents, I don't recall them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the same time, tell us, please, Mr. Maric, and we are talking about the first half of 1993, what the safety situations, security situation, was in the Town of Busovaca itself? Was there shooting? Were there grenades or was the situation peaceful?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, the situation was perhaps a little better in town than it was along the defence line because in the municipal building, for example, that is where I usually worked, we were not, our safety was not always assured there as the town was being shelled across the road from the municipal building, that is to say 10 to 15 metres a grenade fell in the vicinity, so nobody felt quite safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilian casualties in the Town of Busovaca itself?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, of course, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many people were wounded or killed in the Town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Maric, the municipal building that you mentioned a moment ago, where is it located within Busovaca itself? Is it along the periphery or is it in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, it's in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the attacks from the surrounding villages with a predominantly Muslim population in the direction of Busovaca, could you tell us how far those villages are situated from the Town of Busovaca itself, as the crow flies for example?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, it's very near. Well, let's say 1.000 metres, 1.500, 1.000 metres, 2.000 metres, not very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, would I be wrong in saying that at that time, during the combat activities in 1993, the area of the Municipality of Busovaca was more or less equally just as safe and secure in comparison to the combat activities?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there one particular locality in Busovaca or its surroundings which was quite safe from the fighting?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, that did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go back for a moment to the work units. What was the national composition of those work units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The national composition, ethnic composition, was there were Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Maric, did you, when selecting individuals for these units, bear in mind who you were going to select in view of their age and in view of their health or some other reasons, for example?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, yes, when we would send an invitation to these people, a call up, all those had to join. At the time, we would look at their psychophysical condition generally, and how old they were, and what they would be capable of doing, what work they would be capable of doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If, for example, a recruit would supply you with medical, a medical report which would say that his health was not good enough for work, did you take account of this?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, until his treatment, medical treatment was completed. We would not take in people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, although you said in your introduction that you are a machine technician, are you acquainted with the provisions and regulations to be applied in performing your duties subsequently?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, they were provisions and regulations dating back to the former Yugoslavia which were taken over by Bosnia-Herzegovina and the provision on the organisation and implementation of work duties for total national defence, which the executive council of Bosnia-Herzegovina enacted in 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, this is a regulation enacted by Bosnia-Herzegovina and was therefore applied throughout the territory?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, because we had no other regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, from your personal contacts, whether these same regulations would be applied to the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was at that time controlled by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No? I'm sorry, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: When the war ended and the Croats left Zenica, they said that they did the same kind of work, they dug trenches along the defence lines and so these regulations were also applied there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, until when did you perform your tasks on civil defence in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: About the 15th of June, 1993, up to then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I went to join the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many people were employed in the work that you were doing?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Very few. There were four of us employed in this civil defence work in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When we spoke about the call ups of the conscripts to perform the work duties, you said that this was, for the most part, done by sending couriers with the call up notice, if circumstances allowed, and, if not, that the military police would be used to collect these people?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Maric, whether individual military commanders along the defence lines also applied this direct form of call up using the military police or was this not a practice?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, they did, directly, if the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When was that? You say "When the need arose," what did you have in mind there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, when there were extensive combat activities and when it was not, there was not enough time to organise everything in the normal run of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, tell us, please, whether you know the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the intention of that facility was when it was built and what happened later on with that facility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, it was a barracks of the Yugoslav Peoples Army. At least that's as much as we knew about it then because as it was a barracks, we were not allowed to approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The army of the former Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav Peoples Army, left Bosnia-Herzegovina somewhere in mid-1992. That is the first half of 1992, if I am not mistaken. What happened to Kaonik after that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, after that, Kaonik was taken over by the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For what purpose? What existed there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, the army was there. That is to say part of the HVO units were located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that one of the buildings in the Kaonik facility was refurbished and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, one of the barracks buildings became a prison, was turned into a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time when this building was rearranged, did you visit it?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Maric, whether in the locality around Kaonik, at the beginning of the conflict in Busovaca, whether the inhabitants of Busovaca of the Muslim nationality were sent there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I know that they were put up there. That means that all those citizens of Busovaca who did not respond to the call up, their military call up, or had done something else, were sent to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you visit these people in Kaonik ever?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you in some other way have contacts with those individuals?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Maric, what the population was there? Were they people who were conscripts or were they some other people?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, they were conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the municipality, in the defence department, did you have any records of those people as being recruits and conscripts?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you find those records when you came?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, is it correct if I say that at that time, there were no records on these individuals as conscripts in the municipality? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said in your introduction that when you took up your duties in the civil defence department in Busovaca, you found that the records of the Muslim recruits were for the most part taken away. Now as these are also people of the Muslim nationality, did you have any records on those people in the municipality or not?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, we did not have any records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know why these individuals were sent to the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: As I said, probably they had -- this was a disciplinary action for not -- they could not remain at home. Everybody had to do some work, so if anybody refused to do some work, then they would be sent there, even old people work and old women, so it was inadmissible that conscripts were allowed to go scot-free and do nothing. Of course it would be difficult to ask them to fight against their own people and that is why they were sent to the detention centre where their ethnicity would not be in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Maric, that in performing your civil defence duties, had never had contact with these people from the Kaonik facilities; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No -- yes, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who it was, not his name, but what organisation was authorised to call upon these people in the Kaonik camp to perform their duties?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, it was the HVO command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From your experience and from your recollections, can you tell us of an incident that occurred when these individuals performed their work duties; do you know anything about that or not?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know, Mr. Maric -- let me ask the question in a different way. You said that the beginnings of the conflicts in Busovaca were somewhere around the 24th of January, do you know when these individuals from Busovaca were taken to Kaonik? Immediately after the fighting, before or after?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know when they returned from Kaonik? Is that something that you're acquainted with?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you spent some time in the region, you are acquainted with the situation that existed there, you said that from the direction of Kacuni and other directions the attacks were launched of the BH Army on Busovaca. What do you think in view of the fact that you performed your civil defence duties and that you took part in the army as a volunteer, what was the military goal of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The military goal of the attacks launched was to, for these forces to take over Busovaca and to set up a Muslim state of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is Busovaca and its municipality located along an important communications line?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, between Sarajevo, Kiseljak, Travnik, Bugojno, Split. That is the main communication line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that communication line in the military sense important or is it peripheral?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time in the military sense, was it important who was in control of that communication line?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You personally took part in the defence of the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca, did you not? Can you tell us from your own experience whether you ever undertook any offensive drives to take over territory outside the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary, we only defended our own part, our own villages and houses where my family was located, so we had no offensive drives whatsoever. We just protected our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In those conflicts, in the fighting, Mr. Maric, did you ever notice that on the side of the defence, that is you who had put up a defence, that other soldiers, apart from the HVO and the local population took part?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I never saw anybody of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you in quite concrete terms, did you see any soldiers with insignias of the HV, the army of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, never. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the fact that in the Lasva River Valley, soldiers of the Croatian army took part?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you some more general, just a few more general questions, regarding life and work there at the time. Would it be true to say that during these wartime circumstances, the Municipality of Busovaca was encircled, in an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, it was under total encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that communications towards outside from the municipality were severed?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you tell us what the supply situation was like? Food? Fuel? Heating? Weapons? How did this function?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, supplies were based on humanitarian organisations, the Red Cross brought us food. Caritas, and other humanitarian organisations. Whereas the rest, everybody had to fend for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about the population? Was there enough clothing, footwear, food to go around?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were these conditions the same for everybody or were parts of the population favoured, for example, the army?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, everybody was in the same boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Maric, that you were in Kaonik did you -- no, I'm sorry, you said that you had never been to Kaonik. But did you have occasion to meet the warden of the military prison in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, I know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you point him out in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, over there. (Witness indicated)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The witness had shown in the direction of the accused as somebody who he knows under the name of Zlatko Aleksovski. I am now going to ask you, Mr. Maric, whether you met Mr. Aleksovski in Busovaca in the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were the personal driver of the president of the HVO for the Municipality of Busovaca, what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: His name is Zoran Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us then, having mentioned the HVO, is the HVO a civilian or a military organisation? Is it a civilian or military body? Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: What I know is that the Croatian Defence Council, which meant that the staff had become the Croatian Defence Council to become the Croatian army. The chief of staff. Whereas the Croatian Defence Council within the frameworks of the municipality was within the frameworks of the municipality and the civilian department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that the Croatian Defence Council was a body who had both civilian and military components within itself?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And being guided by the fact that the president of the HVO was a civilian for Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this civilian the president of the Croatian Defence Council in the Municipality of Busovaca, did he have any authorisations towards the military formations and units? Could he issue orders to these units? Could he be in command as a civilian or did he have other duties to perform?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, I don't think he commanded the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann, or Mr. Meddegoda maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you said a while ago that you functioned in the capacity as civilian defence commander until the 15th of June, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And then you said you joined the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Which of the units did you join thereafter?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And in which area, which operative zone were those units which you joined based?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: In Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that zone in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: That time? I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who was immediate commander, the commander of your unit which you joined, which unit that you joined?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Mr. Jure Cauran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what role did you perform in those units that you joined?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Duties that were asked of me. That means whatever I was asked to do, which was asked at that time for that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what were the duties that were asked of you at that time?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: To regularly carry out the duties ordered to me by my superior commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Maric, I know they were the duties that the commanders asked you to do, I am asking you what were those duties that you were entrusted by those commanders?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer this question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Why not? Why can't you answer the question? Is that it that you don't remember those duties or is it that you can't answer the question?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Those were the duties of a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did those soldiers' duties involve? Did those soldiers' duties involve fighting in the front?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, just defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Defence. And where were you defending?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Together with you, how many soldiers were in your unit which were defending Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how many could you recall? Was it 10 or 15 or 100 or more?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: About 1.500, somewhere around 1.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how many of those 1.500 soldiers were soldiers belonging to your unit, the unit that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you, when you say the majority, your unit had soldiers numbering about, anything between 750 to 1.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And if you could help me, Mr. Maric, who did you say your commander was? That is the commander of your unit.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The brigade commander was Mr. Cauran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who was your immediate commander, the commander of the unit to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who did you report for duty, when you had to take leave, when you had to absent yourself from duty, whose permission would you generally obtain?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who was that commander?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Zarko Soskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And the brigade commander you said was Mr. Travcic, was it?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: He was the head commander of the brigade in Busovaca, as you said?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long prior to your duty, how long prior to you joining the HVO was Mr. Travcic the commander of the brigade; do you know?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it a few days, a couple of weeks?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I cannot really lay out the dates for you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the dates, Mr. Maric, what I want to know is how long before you joined the unit did the brigade commander take up duty, have taken up duty as the commander of the brigade in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Defence is compelled to respond to this line of questioning of my learned colleague. We need to point out that the questions regarding the composition of the military units which were stationed at Busovaca are outside of the scope of the indictment, as well as the examination-in-chief of the Defence. We believe that it is not pertinent what type of military units were in Busovaca, because the indictment only points to Kaonik and activities there. So we believe that these, this line of questioning goes outside of the scope of the examination, and we object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Mikulicic is quite right; however, one must also bear in mind that these questions have also direct link with the credibility of the witness. Mr. Meddegoda, bearing this in mind, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, as I said, I will repeat my question. I'm not interested in the date on which the brigade commander assumed duty. What I want to know is, you said you joined the HVO units on the 15th of June 1993; how long before that, when was it that brigade commander had assumed duty, in charge of the brigade, how many days prior to your joining the HVO unit, how many weeks or months prior to your joining the HVO units had the commander assumed duty as commander of the brigade in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Perhaps, perhaps in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. And for how long did you continue to work in the HVO unit Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how are you employed, Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I work in the Media Plan tile factory in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Going back to early '93 late '92, Mr. Maric, you said there was tension building up in the area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was at that time that you joined the defence units of the HVO as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: More precisely, I was a driver to the HVO president. I was his personal driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But you became the personal driver only sometime in January, in the early part of 1993; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And before that, you functioned in the HVO as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you were involved in the defence of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were the tensions? Could you describe to this court what incidents took place in the area of Busovaca in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: In late 1992, that is when the Serbian aggression against the area of Ravno started in 1991. Since that time the HVO got involved as much as it could, and then this Muslim population did not get involved. Only later on, after the immediate threat of war was declared in April of 1992, and in late 1992 the tensions started building up in a sense, that is between the HVO and these people, because they were not getting involved. They would not become involved in securing the facilities which were important at that time, like communication lines and bridges and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, it was by late 1992 that the tension started building up between the HVO and the Muslim people of the area?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, the Muslim population. This tension was felt in the sense that the conscripts of the Muslim army, of the Muslim units did not take part in providing security in the area of Busovaca, which was covered by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I mean what did they do if they did not take part in securing the area? What did the Muslim people do instead of taking part in securing the area?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: For the most part, to my knowledge, they were concentrated in their own smaller groups, in their villages and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And perhaps the Muslims did not want to fight in the Republic of Croatia, did not want to fight along with the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was at this time that, as you said earlier on in your evidence, that the Muslim people males, women and children, men, women and children, all started leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I mean, you being an inhabitant, a native of Busovaca municipality, you would have known these Muslim people from your childhood.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were they neighbours of yours also that left the area during this time during the tension that was prevalent?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, my village, village where I live. The village where I live had combined Croatian and Serbian population and there was a Muslim village about seven or eight hundred metres away from my village, so we did not have such close contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you know, did you happen to know the Muslim people from the area of Busovaca? You studied in the elementary school there, and did you happen to know the people of the area, your friends, the school friends, your acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I did not go to school in Busovaca, I went to Katici; but I knew them from Merdani and other places like Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And if you may proceed, and you said there was a Muslim village about seven to eight hundred metres away from your village; that village I presume was predominantly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Merdani? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And Muslims from that village, what position did they take, what stand did they take at this time when the tension was building up?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: For the most part these encounters were infrequent. Any larger gathering, there were no larger gatherings anymore, so these encounters were kind of sporadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You, Mr. Maric, you said that you, after some time functioning in the volunteer units of the HVO, you were appointed the driver of the HVO president of the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And then it was Mr. Zoran Maric?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Is he a relation of yours or is he connected to you?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How is he connected to you?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: He is my first cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, it was because of your relationship, I mean, he considered you to be a trusted and loyal person and that was why he appointed you, he took you as his driver, personal driver.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: He probably had his own reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But he was also, he would have, I believe, considered the fact that you were his relation and therefore he could rely on you and trust you and also rely on your loyalty.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was during this time that, after this, it was in March that you were appointed the commander of the civilian protection, civilian defence in Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who appointed you commander of civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The HVO president, Zoran Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was there a decree appointing you as commander of civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, by a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The presidency of the Croatian defence council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what were your duties and responsibilities as commander of civilian defence in the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I already mentioned that. The duties and obligations of the commander of the civilian protection included organisation of the activities, to organise the activities and reception, primarily, of the large numbers of the refugees in the area of Busovaca; as well as to establish the work units; as well as all other activities that issue from it, that regard the organisation of civilian life, such as fire department, assistance to certain economic facilities and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how many work units were established under your command in the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How many work units did you have, or how many work units were composed when you took over as commander, when you were appointed as commander of civilian defence? You said one of your functions was to establish work units; how many work units did you establish when you were in authority, in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: There may have been, maybe two or three work units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And how would you enlist people for such work units? Would you describe to us the procedure of enlisting people for such work units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: All military conscripts who did not have war time assignments were sent to the work units of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have the list of names of all the people, military conscripts who were to be assigned to such work units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I said that there was, that I did not find a list of the Muslim conscripts; and so, through the people's defence office, I did compile such a list; and on the basis of that, I compiled a list for the work unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, forgive me for interrupting. I think we should now take a break. This would allow everyone to take a rest. Let us take a 20-minute break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, before the recess I was asking you about the procedure in which you compiled a list for the work units. And you said that these lists were compiled and that the list of Muslim conscripts, you obtained them from the peoples defence office?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The call up, that is compiling of the list went through the peoples defence office to the people who would be called up by the peoples defence office. And this was of the military conscripts in the territory of Busovaca municipality. But we did compile a new list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who compiled that list in your office, in the civilian defence office? Was it done by you or was it done by anybody else?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I compiled it myself. So, I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The list so compiled, the persons in those lists, you said you had divided them into about two to three work units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was the procedure when you required, when you had to enlist the services of those people for particular, specific types of work?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: At the request of the commander of a unit or the HVO commander, for a particular type of work, they requested a certain number of people. And based on such a request, we would call these military conscripts from the work unit and then we would form one such work unit and we would send it out in the field to perform the particular type of task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: From whom the commander, a unit commander or the HVO commander, request for a certain number of people? To whom would such commander, the unit commander, or the HVO commander make such request?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They would send it to the civilian defence, that is to the commander of the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And then in your case, in the Busovaca municipality, it would be addressed to you, that request would be addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: From the time, the time that you functioned as a commander of civilian defence from March, from mid-March of 1993, to about the 15th of June, 1993, how many such requests were addressed from you from the unit commanders or from the HVO commanders?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I believe somewhere around 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then when there was a request addressed to you by a unit commander, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I would carry it out and I would call the certain number of the conscripts and I would send them to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you would request them in writing, or at times you would send courier or a messenger to those people, to join in the work unit?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: We would send these calls through the couriers and we would execute them or serve them through a military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I believe these were written requests that were sent to them? They were sent in writing?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What would happen to a person to whom such a request was sent, wasn't at home at the time the request was sent?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: A second call or request would be sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was that a report back to you from the military police about the execution of that request?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes. They would report, for instance, that he was not home. They couldn't find him or he was not at that address, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: All such requests would go under your hand as civilian defence commander?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Maric, that there were in the course of your, in the course of your period of duty as civilian defence commander, there were about ten requests that you received from HVO commanders, how many of such requests concerned trench digging on the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: For the most part these requests concerned these work on digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall how many of such requests were connected with digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: There were maybe six or seven such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were the other three or four requests, what were those requests for?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The other requests concerned working on clearing the area right next to the frontline, so assistance to the fire department, to the humanitarian organisations, to utility companies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Maric, a while ago you said that you compiled a list yourself and on those lists that are compiled, did you have names of Bosniaks of most people of Muslims at the city who were on that lists that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Of course there were all three groups, Bosniak Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what is the approximate percentage of Bosniaks who were in the list that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Somewhere around 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now whenever a request is made, you said you would send, whenever a request is received by you, you would send an HVO military police to collect the people and then what would you do?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Those people would assemble at a particular meeting point in town. They would be told what their work duty was and then they were transported to the location where they were supposed to do this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would tell them what their work duty was?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It would usually be myself what their work duty was or the immediate commander at the line of defence where they were supposed to carry out this work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now would you go with the persons with the work unit to the place where the work duty was supposed to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: If my duties allowed me to, yes, I would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: There were instances that you did go, you went to such places where work duty was carried out?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Kula, Podjele and Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was the work in Kula and in Podjele and Loncari where the work units, what type of work that they had to perform on the occasions that you went along with the work unit?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: This was digging of trenches, dugouts, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long would each work unit work for?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It all depended on the type of work which was to be performed. So this work could take anywhere from four to eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who would determine that the length of work that each work unit was to perform?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: For the most part it was the needs at this frontline of how much it needed to be fortified. And, on the basis of that, that determined how many people and how many hours were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were the people on the frontlines when they were working digging trenches and dugouts and building fortifications? Do you know the conditions under which they worked?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, there were conditions ensuring their safety. That is to say they worked at night and always when there were no combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were they fed? Were they given drink?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, they were fed like the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, now you, I presume -- I withdraw that question, Your Honours. Mr. Maric, you said that the HVO units were involved primarily in the defence of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You did not participate, that your units did not participate in any offensive actions in that area?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Perhaps, are you aware that the HVO did conduct offensive actions in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: If there was fighting, it was to defend the area and the main communication lines. That is to say, the road between Busovaca, Travnik, Bugojno and so on. That was in the service of the defence of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it in the defence of the area that the HVO units attacked Ahmici in the month of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: First of all, the HVO did not attack Ahmici, the HVO defended Ahmici in order to retain the Busovaca/Travnik communication line, Vitez and so on, Bugojno and Split, on to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it is your position that the HVO did not attack Ahmici at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It was all in the service of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So an attack did take place and your position is that that attack was in the defence of the area that the offensive actions took place?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It was an attack by the Muslim forces on the main communication line and on the HVO localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you also know that acts took place in the Village of Marici (phoen) in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect, I have an objection to make of my learned colleague, the Prosecutor. We are talking about military operations which were not included in the indictment and the military actions that are witness did not take part in. So that these questions do not have nothing to do with the indictment nor with the credibility of the witness. If we are once again evaluating the credibility of the witness, then this can be done within the frameworks of the facts contained in the indictment. That is the form that my objection takes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness very categorically in the course of his evidence has stated that there were no offensive actions conducted by the HVO during the early part of 1993. That was his position. He has taken up the position that they were only defensive actions. It is my endeavour to show to him, to establish before Your Honours' Court, that the HVO did, in fact, during the period that he is talking, did, in fact, conduct offensive actions and was not only involved in defending the area, but also did in fact conduct offensive actions. That is, therefore, the purpose of the cross-examination in putting these questions to this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We have heard what the witness has said. The witness said that the HVO had attacked Ahmici in order to defend its position in Busovaca. So, Mr. Meddegoda, please put questions to the witness that are more directly linked to what has happened in Kaonik. It seems to me that, in fact, the witness himself said that he had had to attack Ahmici in order to defend Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you also said in the course of your evidence this morning, Witness, you know what Kaonik camp was during the JNA times, during the JNA period?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that it was later refurbished for some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How do you know that it was refurbished?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: First, because the HVO was there, so that means that after the Yugoslav Peoples Army had left the barracks, the barracks were taken up by the HVO and I was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you posted at Kaonik at any point in time when you were a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I was not. I was on the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, but had you -- did you have any direct duty in the Kaonik complex within the Kaonik facility as a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Have you ever been situated at the Kaonik facility either as a member of the HVO or in the course of your duties as a civilian defence commander?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: As a member of the HVO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When was that that you were situated at the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by camp. It was a barracks of the former Yugoslav Peoples Army and then it was a barracks of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Okay. When did you visit the barracks of the HVO in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The HVO barracks, a part of the command was stationed there and that's when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you, before 1994, you have not visited the Kaonik, the HVO barracks in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So during the period of 1992 and 1993, you did not visit the HVO barracks in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So how do you know that the Kaonik facility was refurbished at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: By talking to my colleagues, to my friends, I know that up there a building was being adapted as a detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What did your colleagues tell you about the building that was being erected as a detention centre?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Nothing special, just that the building was going to be used as a detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So then when you said that you knew that it was refurbished, that was not correct? You only learned that it was to be used as a detention centre, that is all?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you went on to say that in this detention centre, people were detained during 1993?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I learned about this talking to my colleagues and the people that I had occasion to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who are the colleagues whom you spoke to, from whom you learned about people being detained in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: My friends, which means my colleagues from the line, defence line, and in talking to the people, everybody knew that Kaonik was intended to work as a detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who were the people who were detained in the Kaonik detention centre?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They were all those people who did not respond to their military call up or had done something else, another violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now as regards to those persons who did not respond to the military call up, do you know who sent them to the Kaonik detention facility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know when this military call up was?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
