utterances.text: It was when I drew up, compiled the lists for civilian defence and the defence department called up all the population to take up their military operation duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So that was after March of 1993, after the 15th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That was the time that civilian defence was established? It was first established in March of 1993 when you were appointed commander of civilian defence. There were no lists compiled before the 15th of March, 1993; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: It probably existed, but with the reorganisation that was taking place and the fact that the members of the Muslim nationality had left, then the work of the civilian defence units was not, did not undergo continuity, so during that period, this was done, but the need arose for new commanders of civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then you were appointed commander of civilian defence and you drew up a list of people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So it was from those lists that the people you say were sent to the Kaonik detention facility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who sent them to the Kaonik detention facility? On whose orders were they sent there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: The lists I had, the names I had on my list, those people were there. All of them were there. And on the basis of those requests, I made a new list of the people who were in the Municipality of Busovaca and these people from Kaonik, some of them were on the list that I had in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes. Well my question to you is, who sent those people to the Kaonik detention facility?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: If they refused to respond to the call up and perform their duties, so if he refused to respond two or three times, then we would send them, hand the matter over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there such persons who did not respond to your call two or three times?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No, usually they did respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Which means there were no people who were sent to the Kaonik detention facility for evading military duty or conscription?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: While I worked, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You wouldn't know what happened while you were not civilian defence commander, would you?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you also said that there were others who were sent there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who were those others, and for what were they sent there?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They were others like people of the Serbo-Croat nationality that did not respond to the call, perhaps they liked alcohol too much. Anybody who did not correspond to the needs at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, but during your time as civilian defence commander, you said a while ago that people responded to the cause for civilian defence, and you agreed there were no such people who were sent to the Kaonik facility for detention for evading military duty?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: From the list that I had, the people did respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, your microphone was switched off so that the interpreters did not hear you. Could you repeat what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I have no further questions in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Meddegoda. Mr. Mikulicic, any further questions you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, perhaps just several questions to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Juric, I beg your pardon, Mr. Maric, you answered some questions put to you by the Prosecutor which were raised regarding the work units formed at the time when you worked in the civilian defence section, and you said that there were two to three work units, and that on ten or so occasions they were called up for duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Maric, whether these two to three work groups that you mentioned earlier on were, according to their composition, permanent work groups, or did they change in composition? Were the people that made up those units always the same or change according to circumstance?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They changed according to circumstance, the composition changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you mentioned that on ten or so occasions you received requests for engaging work units, do you know whether those work units were engaged in some other way outside the realm of your civilian defence department by the commanders themselves?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, for example, the command or the commanders could engage a work unit themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know on how many occasions this occurred, if we look at the ten or so cases that you mentioned which were under the jurisdiction of civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you spoke about the call ups for recruits to the work units, you said that these call ups were done either via courier or by the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In the case of urgency, when this had to be a speedy process, did you also use couriers, or did you seek other ways and means which would be faster under the given circumstances?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, in these very urgent cases when there was no time to send a courier and a normal call up, then we would resort to using the military police to collect the recruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. Mr. Maric, did you personally, as an inhabitant of the Municipality of Busovaca, have occasion to see individuals who were interned in the Kaonik camp do any labour?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion I saw them up by the bridge near my house in Kaonik Podjele, it was a bridge they were applying a new layer of concrete to. So, going home I saw them working on the bridge. I knew some of them and I would talk to some of them, and I learned that they were at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did they perform these duties under supervision or without supervision?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: They performed this duty under the supervision of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, the Defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I have a few questions I would like to put to you. You have told us about these lists of people who were supposed to work in these work units. You told us that at a particular time you had realised that this list had disappeared. Were there any separate lists, separate lists bearing the name of people from different ethnic groups, or was there only one list?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: No separate lists, there was just one list of all the ethnic denominations, Muslims, Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you well. It seems to me that you said that only the list bearing the Muslim names had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, there was only one list, or was there a number of separate lists?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Not a list in fact, the list was a joint one; but records, we had records for civilian defence that existed, and all the cards in the records with the Muslim population was missing, all the files relating to the Muslim population were missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, on that list the name of the Muslim persons did not appear; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: At that particular moment in the department for civilian defence, it did not exist. But via the defence department, which did have the files, we were able to supplement our lists with the help of those files and records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another thing, do you know if the prisoners in the Kaonik camp were sent to dig trenches on their own or were they accompanied by other work units?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I think they went alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, do you know, are you familiar with the uniforms with the insignias bourne by the Croatian soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: These uniforms, these insignias were similar to or quite dissimilar from the uniforms insignia bourne by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: For the most part they were different particularly for the insignia HV and the insignia HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You said in general they were not similar to the other uniforms; but in specific cases, could these different uniforms show some similarity, were they similar in some way?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I don't think -- only according to form. They were clearly distinguishable, just the shape different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I understand. But the people who were familiar with these slight differences could establish the difference you're speaking of; but could it happen that a person who was not familiar with these differences, would it happen that such a person could confuse these uniforms, could think that they were people from the HV, when in fact they were people from the HVO, and the other way around?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Well, no, because you could clearly distinguish the HV from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another thing, you said that during a certain period of time there were no clothes, no shoes around to be found. Did it happen that sometimes the HVO soldiers did not bear insignias?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, it did happen that the HVO soldiers did not bear any insignias, because there were no insignias to be distributed; is that right? Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible, because under the circumstances there was not enough uniforms of this kind to go around, or insignia to go around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You also said that you, yourself, had gone to a certain number of places to escort the work units. When you went to these places, did you see the facilities where the prisoners coming from Kaonik were held?

utterances.speaker: Viktor Maric
utterances.text: I said that I saw some of them along the lines towards the bridge, towards Podjele, I did not go on the spot, however. But for the most part where the civilian defence units were working, I did not come across them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. I don't think we have any further questions for you Mr. Maric. Thank you very much for coming to testify before this Tribunal. Have a safe journey home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to thank you, too. 19 (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think you wish to call another witness to the stand, but maybe we should take a break now, 15-minute break now. This will enable us to start with direct examination of the witness immediately after the break, we would not have to interrupt the direct examination of the witness. Do you agree with this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We shall now take a 15-minute break and then start with the examination of the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Neimann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just raise a matter before the next witness is called. I noticed in respect of this witness it would seem that he holds a position equivalent to the position of the last witness within the Municipality of Vitez, and to that extent presumably is somewhat similar to the witness Rajic which we already heard from, who has a position in the Municipality of Travnik. But the point I raise, Your Honour, is about the relevance of another witness from another municipality being called by the Defence, especially in circumstances where they have already called the witness from Busovaca, which was the area directly connected to and related to Kaonik. And I am prompted to do this Your Honour, because Mr. Mikulicic tends to object when we move beyond the scope of the indictment or beyond the Kaonik camp, as such, and has done so on numerous occasions, and it would seem that this is perhaps a similar situation that he accuses the Prosecution of becoming involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. I would like to clarify what the intention of the Defence is in regard of presentation of testimony of these witnesses. The Municipalities of Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca are in the Lasva River Valley, which are about five to ten kilometres away from one another. And so, they are all part of the Lasva River Valley, which is a part of the indictment. It was isolated during the pertinent period of time here, and so, they all lived under similar circumstances. The idea of the Defence is to present witnesses from these three areas and to show what the practices were during the pertinent period of time covered in the indictment. For instance, the Defence has called these witnesses in order to show how the work duty functioned in the territory of the, not only of Busovaca, but also the neighbouring municipalities which were in the Lasva River Valley. And the Defence would like to point out that the organisation was very similar with very minor differences. So, that is one purpose. Another purpose is to present to the Honourable Trial Chamber and our colleagues what the use of the work units was. And I believe that this is one of the key issues as regards the charges against my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let us hear the witness. We will bear in mind the fact that there is no need to repeat information or questions that have been put to previous witnesses. Questions have to be as direct as possible, let us not lose any time. Need I remind you we need to close this case as quickly as possible, we need to have precise information. If some questions have already been put to other witnesses and have received answers by these questions, then there is no need to put them again to this witness. Do we all agree on that? If so, the next witness may be called in. Mr. Neimann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence calls the witness Dragan Strbac. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strbac, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now read the solemn declaration that the usher is holding out for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated. For the moment being, I will ask you to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, the gentleman on your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Strbac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I represent the accused and I will ask you questions in that respect and ask you to respond to them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Strbac when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I was born on 29 July, 1963 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you go to school, elementary school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I graduated from the elementary school in Dubravica in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a religious person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: It is Catholic religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After completing the elementary school, did you go to another school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the high school in Vitez. After the graduation I enrolled in the metallurgical school at the university in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where you were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, in 1982 I went in October to serve in Banja Luka, and after that I was transferred in February of 1993. And I returned home on the 8th of October of '93 (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I heard you say that, you said '82, so you would have finished in '83?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, it was '83.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you acquire a rank?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, not a rank, I just became a specialist, I became a tank driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you take employment after you were released from the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, as I said, I enrolled in the metals engineering school, which I graduated from in 1988, and then I waited for a couple of years until I found a job, and I finally found employment in '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was your employment during that period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I was in charge of the civilian protection in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When was that, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on, in 1992, did you also work in the same job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the same post throughout. I was the chief of the civilian protection of the Municipality of Vitez, so that was my professional duty. And after the conflict with the Bosniak Muslim side, I also assumed the position of chief of the civilian protection, which was a voluntary position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, you had two functions, one was professional and one was voluntary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, for one you were paid, you received a salary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And as a commander of the civilian protection, that was a volunteer type of position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before you took over this post in 1993, who was the commander of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: It was Sulejman Smreko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnic group this person was from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened such that he stopped working there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: When the conflict started in April of 1993 between the HVO and the then Territorial Defence, or as they call it, the army of the BH, Mr. Smreko did not see fit, and I must say that we didn't see it, either, fit for him to continue in this position. And in this period of the month of April he was still in Vitez, he continued to live in his apartment where I visited him on several occasions. We had a couple of conversations in that regard, and he personally considered that it would not be right for him to continue in this position. So, I took over as commander of the civilian protection staff. And I must say on this occasion that after about one month after this start of the conflict, at his personal request, and with our assistance, he moved to the territory of Zenica municipality. And I don't know if I should add this, even though I personally was trying to convince him to stay, he said that he wanted to go where all his people went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how it was, how he was able to go to Zenica? Were there communication lines open?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, we helped him through UNPROFOR, the international forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you meet him later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, I personally did not, but persons who were my subordinates did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: During the period of time when some part of the units were clearing the terrain in the area called Mahala where the majority of the population was Muslim. So, during this clearing of the terrain, during the period, during the time when dead bodies were being recovered from the area, one of my staff met him, and it seemed a bit strange to us how come that he had gone to Zenica and now we saw him here in this area. And I'm not sure, we had some information which I was unable to corroborate that he was commander of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say commander, what forces do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: This would be the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, you said you grew up in Dubravica, is that part of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is it from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: About 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you in the village of Dubravica throughout this period of conflict? That is, the area where you grew up where your parents were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: On the third day, the Muslim forces took my village and they set my house on fire first, and this area is still under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened to your family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: We were expelled. We found refuge in the city. One bedroom apartment to eight family members, so you can imagine what kinds of conditions we live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, is the Vitez municipality in the town of Vitez a neighbouring municipality to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you, in your work, contact and cooperate with your colleagues in Busovaca with the colleagues who were involved in similar types of work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, when the conditions allowed that, but it was becoming difficult in the -- maybe in the second part of 1993, but let's say until July, very little, because risks were very high. It was very difficult to go from one municipality to another, to leave your own area, because the situation was very delicate. It was a valley where you could shoot from one end to another very easily. So the risk was very high and one did not want to run them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said that you were both the chief and commander of the civilian protection. What was your job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: My job was to organise the civilian protection, to put it at disposal of the civilian population, to protect it. It is a way to organise civilian population against the elemental disasters and war damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, how did this civilian protection work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: In the Municipality of Vitez, we had municipal staff of civilian protection where I was chief and, as I mentioned earlier, also commander. And I had my assistants for certain -- in certain fields, which means an assistant for first medical aid. I am only going to enumerate certain ones. It would be for protection against fire, rescue from destroyed structures, protection of vegetation, of animals, of animal stock, animal feed and so on. And the civilian -- so these were the measures that we would take. However, we also organised units of civilian protection. We had specialised units, which would be the units which were engaged in specific activities, like first aid, fire protection and so on. And the units for general use, which were engaged in all other activities, which were dictated by the circumstances on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, what was the legal foundation? Were there legal provisions for the civil protection? And I am not asking you to quote them all, but did you have them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Before the conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we had a particular system and this system was based on certain legal provisions. And specifically in this area, we used the law and defence of the former SFRY, which was adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And on the basis of these documents, we organised civilian protection in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these regulations were in force throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were also general purpose units in the civilian protection, can you tell us what was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I have given you some specialised names that we gave to certain of those, but there were work units, so these were units which were used for anything which needed to be done in order to organise normal life in an area. So, whatever the population needed. I am not talking about any specific tasks, they could do anything which the competent authority or the competent body would request of us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that these work units could also be used to support the military units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: As I said, anything that had to do with the defence and continuation of life there, so they could do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know whether these work units, which were subordinated to you, involved in activities relating to the defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How was this organised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: We in Vitez organised it in such a way that the office for peoples' defence would call up the conscripts. And I am going to call them conscripts because they were part of the work units. So we established these work units with commanders and then these units would be sent out to perform a task wherever we got the request from. For instance, for fortification of the defence lines -- I am giving an example. If we couldn't, we would usually compile a list of the conscripts. Since this was a wartime situation, we would usually give this list to a military policeman and then he would make rounds to the indicated addresses, to these persons. He advises the conscript to report at a certain location at a given time, to report to his commander. And from there on, the commander would take over the control of these conscripts and then would take the conscripts to wherever the task needed to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, who were the conscripts? Now we're talking about the work duty, who were the conscripts for the work duty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: These were the persons who were not able to be conscripted by the armed forces. So whoever, the part of the population which could not be used for military purpose, we used in work units and other civilian protection units, whoever was able to contribute to the defence with respect to work units and civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, can you give me about the ethnic composition, was anything specific there or were these work units established regardless of the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: These units were established according to the territorial principles. So the ethnic group was not a factor there. And I believe that this is the best principle, the territorial principle. So that the people in such conditions would run the least risk. If we had to transport these people, we would use this territorial principle, so that we could transport them to the location and back with the least risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand, but wasn't it usual that by organising on territorial principles, wasn't it that in certain areas, the Croatian population was prevalent, in another one, Muslims ones, so that certain work units would be composed mostly of Croats and others of mostly Muslims, even gypsies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: That's exactly how it was. I'll give you two examples. In the territory of Vitez municipality, we had an area, which is called Sofa, where the majority population is gypsy. It used to be before the war. It is still the case today. And from the Romali conscripts, we established two work units, let me call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was this the case with some areas where the Muslims were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example of the town. I also had two units there and one unit was predominantly, it consisted mostly of the Muslim conscripts and I had another mixed work unit in town where there were Muslims, Croats and Serbs. And thirdly, I had some units with the majority Croat conscripts, which were organised in areas where the Croatian population was predominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So, in short, it was organised on the territorial principle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, given that this territorial principle resulted in having one ethnic group prevalent in certain units, were they sent to particular areas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, not at all. There were certain specific situations, but they were not unusual for the circumstances in which we lived. If we did not have enough people for a certain situation, we would have to supplement them by units from another area, another one who was free at the time, who had nothing to do at the time. So we did have some needs in certain situations to move one unit from one area to another. So there were no strict rules involved there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, were there situations where you would just attach a work unit to a particular military unit for its needs, and it was then subordinate somehow to this military unit, were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this was the easiest way to go about these things. We had a coordinator, let me call him a coordinator, he was a person who was in charge of a number of these work units. This person coordinated between the office for civilian protection which was calling people up and the military units in order to sort of cut down the time from the time when the group was called up for a certain job until the next time when another need had emerged. Let's say if a certain task required a longer period of time, let's say not one day or one night, then in order for us not to have to waste time to call these people over and over again, because also it was difficult to call people up. The phones were down. There were shelling, so the communication lines were interrupted. So all these made our tasks much more difficult. So we would just agree with the commander at this defence line and we would attach a work unit to this unit in a zone of its responsibility and we would make an arrangement with the commander of this line and commander of the work unit, how they would communicate between one another and how they would supply the transportation and all the other details. So we had such practice to have certain work unit attached to certain military units for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Does that mean that in a situation like this, this particular military commander would be directly responsible both in terms of discipline and organisation for this work unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: As I said, every unit has its own commander. In such a situation, this commander was responsible for the entire situation there, including the work unit, calling up people and, if circumstances allowed, transportation to and from this line of defence and the stay of the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So would this commander also determine what type of work these work units were to perform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We were engaged in any number of activities. But let's say on a frontline, on a defence line, it would be fortification of this frontline, which means building of dugouts, digging of fox holes and trenches and so on. There would also be chopping wood, for instance, and other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Strbac, I think we have clarified this now. Let me ask you the following question: The persons who had work duty and who were called up to join these units, I assume that some of these persons were trying to avoid this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Not only those persons who had work duty. You may be aware that sometimes people tried to avoid not only work duty, but the civilian protection duties as well. This was the case here also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there regulations that provided for the disciplinary measures for such persons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. The law had provisions which regulated these disciplinary infractions, especially in wartime situation where every citizen has a duty to place himself at disposal of the defence forces in a municipality. Every such person who had this legal obligation to perform certain duties, disciplinary measures had to be taken against those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Mikulicic. But it seems to me that we have already heard part of these informations, so could you try to cut it short, could you try to speed things up? Let us try not to repeat things that have already been said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your advice, Your Honour. I think that I have practically reached the end of my questioning. I may just have an additional one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, sir, you said that every citizen had a duty to place himself at disposal of the defence forces. Now I want to ask you who was in charge of it during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: What period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Skopljak was in charge of the defence department office. Would such a person go to perform such a duty as an example?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Mr. Skopljak was not able to do such a thing given his obligations, but through his authority and through his reputation, he certainly gave contribution to stimulate other people. You know, there are always people who find the reasons not to carry out their obligations, but he would use his authority to have such a person to perform his function and give his contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Strbac, just one more question to you and this would end my questioning of this witness. By the nature of your job, you sometimes would go to the frontlines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your visits to the frontlines and your conversations with soldiers who were defending this area, did you ever see any soldier wearing the HV, the Croatian army insignia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: My duties and my job called for constant moving around. I told you that this was risky, but I had to take that risk, so I was constantly on the move. I never saw, I never heard of anybody with the HV insignia. And I wonder how this could happen because we used to say in Vitez that we were like in some kind of a bowl from where nobody could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Strbac, this is my last question and I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann you have the floor. If you have any questions to put to the witness, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Strbac, when you say that you functioned according to the territorial principle, I presume that this changed -- the ethnic composition of the groups changed as the Muslim people left various villages throughout the municipalities of Vitez during the period throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I did not say that I worked, but we organised, which means we organised the recruits for civilian defence according to the territorial principle. And that the ethnical structure with the beginning of the conflicts was upset. I don't think that it was greatly upset. Because a significant portion of the territory of the Municipality of Vitez, where the majority is a Muslim population, it remained under the control of the BH Army and it still remains under its control. All that I can say is that there was a certain drain in the Muslim/Bosniak population, in the centre of the town itself and in one or two villages of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So under the control of the HVO, were there any particular work units over which you had responsibility which were made up of purely Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Let me say, I must say here now that we cannot use the concept of responsible, a responsible military unit and competent because it was not competent for these work units. It's authorisation did not extend there. They performed the function of assisting the military units. They were just a function of the military units; whereas their competence and authorisation only came into being when these units were engaged in some particular actions. So the military units drew up a plan of action. The work units would carry out those plans. Once those plans and that work had been completed, the people would be sent home, disbanded, sent home and would be sent to other work assignments. Of course, via the defence departments and their chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't talking about people being called up and conscripted into military units. I was talking about people being conscripted into civilian work units. And my question to you was: In the area that was under the control of the HVO, in the Vitez area, were there any particular work units, civilian--

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --over which you had responsibility that were made up of purely Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: The work units composed of exclusively Romani people, gypsies I said a moment ago. We had two work units made up of Romani people. And, as I said, they were formed according to the territorial principle and that is why that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we seem to have a communication problem because I wasn't asking about Romani people, I was asking about Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: The Muslims, yes. The Romani are of the Islamic faith in our country and I also said that we had a work unit, which I called Colony Number 1, that was its name. It was a work unit from the town, mostly composed of conscripts. I am not going to say they're civilians. They were conscripts of a work responsibility or civilian protection. They were not civilians. Because if he is a recruit, a conscript, once he has been given his war assignments, that individual becomes either a conscript of civilian protection units or the armed forces. So he would take up his work duties and therefore we did not have civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any Bosnian conscripts in the area of the HVO over which you had responsibility during the period of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did they operate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: The civilian protection units, for example, in the town of Vitez, I had one such unit in charge of humanitarian questions. That is to say it was composed of Muslim, Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs alike, and it was in charge of loading and unloading and distribution of humanitarian relief and supplies. I had another unit where the majority of people were Muslims, Muslim recruits, and that unit was in charge of fortifying the front line. In addition to those two units, I had eight other units of a general purpose with a majority of Croats who also took the fortification work along the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Muslim or Bosniak units, the unit that contained Bosniaks that was used in fortification of the front lines, what front lines were they that you're talking about? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Around the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this was in a front line between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And are you able to give us the names of any of those persons who were Bosniaks who participated in this as a consequence of being called up by you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: They did not work on the basis of my call up. I said that the call up was done by the department for defence. That is the institution authorised to call up conscripts and give out war assignments. The names, I would have to think about that. I had women and men, about 300 conscripts in all. Let me think for a moment. Let me try and remember the commander's name of the Muslim work unit. Karadza Ahmet, for example, he was the commander of the work unit of colony one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And over what period of time was he functioning as the commander of colony one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I think some time between June to February 1994, until the signing of the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was it organised for the commander of a work unit and a military commander to function with each other? Would the commander of the work unit still be responsible for giving directions to the members of his unit, or would that be taken over by the military commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I will. You spoke of the fact that the civilian work units would from time to time work directly for military commanders in the Vitez area. And my question to you is the relationship that then existed between the military commander and the commander of the civilian work unit. Would the commander of the civilian work unit still maintain responsibility for directing these men to work when he was in a situation where he was directly under the control of a military commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: A military commander did not have, as I said a moment ago, the authority to command the work units, or to command the commander of the work unit. He would just issue requests for the defence department to ensure a set number of persons to work in the work units. And on the basis of that request sent in to the department, recruits would be sent. That is as far as we were able to fill those posts. So, he was not in authority to issue orders, but had the possibility of asking, making requests, whether in writing or by telephone, that was not important, and the work units were placed into the service of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, the commander of the work unit was then responsible, I take it, for such things as the safety of his men, for ensuring that they had equipment and things of that nature. Is that true, or correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so, did it work this way: That a military commander would say, "What I would like is for say a trench to be dug here", and once he indicated where it was to be located, it was then a matter for the commander of the work unit to carry out that task with his men in the most efficient way he thought possibly. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I can't tell you what happened along the front line exactly. I was not in authority, I was not present there to see what the work unit did when it came to the front line and what the commander, how the commander issued the request. But I do know that the commanders, via their staff, would issue their requests. Whereas, up on the front line, I don't know what happened. So, the task was, yes, the defence department and civilian protection department in which I worked, I assisted in sending people to carry out their assignments; and when they would get to the particular locality where they were to perform their assignments, then those people would be taken over by the commander of the front line, and he would cooperate with the commander of the front line to see what activities were to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned one of the work units in Vitez was responsible for assisting with humanitarian aid. I take it that this is humanitarian aid that was being brought in by convoy at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these convoys, during the course -- well, 1992 and 1993, fairly regularly came through Vitez; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I would not mix this with 1992. 1992 was something else again, if we compare it to the situation as it was in 1993. In 1993 I can't say that they came regularly. I don't know what you mean by regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly convoys came through Vitez in 1993, anyway.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: From time to time, I would say, periodically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these convoys were organised by the international community, by and large?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes, except the white road convoy, that was in October, if I'm not mistaken, in 1993, where, in the convoy of humanitarian relief, the drive was called the white road, assistance to central Bosnia. And we from the civilian protection department took it upon ourselves to deal with this, regardless of the fact that it was in the area of Nova Bila. From all the regions of the Lasva River valley, members of the civilian protection department took part in the unloading, stocking the relief sent and distributing it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that people who didn't respond to the call up to perform civilian duties could be sent to prison, or imprisoned for doing that. Did that happen at all during the period of time you were in charge of the civilian protection in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: They were placed under detention. I wouldn't say prison. I'm not a legal man, but if we say prison, then this requires a court and so on. I'm not well versed in legal matters, but we call it detention. And let me say that in my own practice, I did not have occasion to send anybody, to apply this disciplinary action and send somebody into detention. Whether others did, I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, so far as you're concerned personally, you didn't have occasion to have to take action against anybody for failure to comply, because the issue had been resolved before it got to that point; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about that portion which was under my authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And you may not know this, because as you said, it didn't arise during your period; but you don't know what law it is that you could have relied on in order to impose disciplinary measures on somebody for evading work, I take it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Disciplinary action, I don't recall what the chapter is called, but the basis is the law on total peoples' defence and social self protection of the Republic of BH, and the chapter relating to disciplinary measures, if somebody, in cases of failure to comply in the armed forces in civilian protection, civil defence, work duties and so on. So it is that particular law which provided for disciplinary action for failure to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period of time in 1993 when you were in Vitez, there were members of the Bosniak population who were being held in detention in Vitez; weren't there, from time to time? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, you never knew of or heard of a situation where civilian Bosniak people were rounded up and held in detention centres in Vitez, in the whole period of time you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I'm not acquainted with that. I didn't hear of anything like that. I don't know the period you have in mind. Are you referring to the entire period of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, the first half of 1993, from January to July of 1993. You never heard of anyone being held in detention centres in Vitez, in cinema complexes, or chess clubs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I'm not acquainted with this. Let me just tell you one thing: With the beginning of the war actions in April, 1993, I did not go home for 15 days, although I performed duties of civilian protection. I'm just giving you this as an illustration. I had so much work to do to protect the civilian population that quite simply I was not able to be informed of military affairs and what was happening elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, if I was to ask you, did you from time to time go to detention centres in order to obtain Bosniak workers to go to the front line and dig trenches, then your answer would be to that, "no", I take it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I, in Vitez, as far as I know, there were no detention centres in Vitez. So, I did not have the possibility of going there. And I don't know why I should. Civilian -- I had no need to go to detention centres, as they did not exist in Vitez, as I say. And I would not have any need to do so, because the number of conscripts that we had, of the number of conscripts that we had, I don't know, I had no need to collect and round up people elsewhere. I don't know where I would go for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you aware of members of the HVO or military police gathering up persons from such centres during the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Which area did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: In Vitez, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to being responsible for organising work units and so forth, were you also involved in arranging housing exchange?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: Let me just tell you one thing: I was not the only person included in organising work units. I said a moment ago, I said how these work units came into being. The department for defence would call up conscripts, give them their war assignments, and I had some work units under my jurisdiction, when they were formed, which means that I was not the sole person responsible. I was just one of the executors. And as far as housing exchange goes, I don't know how at that time, when communications were severed, when all contacts were broken off, how anything could be exchanged, especially houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask the question this way: Did it ordinarily fall under the responsibility or ambit of responsibility of the commander of the civilian defence at any stage to become responsible for organising house exchanges or apartment exchanges?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: No, not under the jurisdiction of civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, the process of exchanging Bosniak houses for Croat houses was not something that you ever engaged in.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN STRBAC
utterances.text: I was included, not in the exchange, the housing exchange, but I was in charge of finding homes for people in the municipality of Vitez, but not housing exchange. On several occasions when the Muslims would leave Vitez, they had some internal agreements with Croats from other municipalities by which they would make agreements and they would ask me to sign those agreements. However, as far as housing exchange is concerned, they were sort of internal agreements amongst these people. They would be signed without any seals or anything of that kind, and as an institution, the civilian protection department was not included in that process. That's all I know about it. So, at that time it was war time, and this was not an essential point. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I received no interpretation, but if I understood you well you have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to put any further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has no questions to put to you Mr. Strbac, thank you very much for coming. We wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, we have still a good half-hour left. Is there another witness that you, that is here that you could call to testify? Because I think that we have the time to listen to yet another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honours, the Defence has no further witnesses, no third witness for today. We were guided by the fact that on the previous days we heard one witness per day. So, we shall conclude there, and tomorrow we will have more witnesses for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I guess the hearing will be adjourned. We understand the situation fully well. We will meet tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m. See you all tomorrow and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
